The ball must be placed between two "hashmarks" each several yards inwards from their respective sidelines. This often results in more open play to one side of the ball. You'll also have ongoing expenses, like food, transportation, and entertainment. You'll have some expenses, like tuition, which doesn't come up every month, but is predictable and needs to be paid. (For these, you'll can set aside part of the money for the expense each month, and when the bill comes, you'll have the funds to pay it ready to go.) Using budgeting software, such as YNAB (which I recommend) will make this whole process much easier. You are allowed to change your plan if you need to at any time, but do not allow yourself to spend any money that is not in the plan. Take action to address any issues that become apparent from your budget. As you do your budget, you will probably struggle, at first. You will find that you don't have enough income to cover your expenses. Fortunately, you are now armed with data to be able to tackle this problem. There are two causes: either your expenses are too high, or your income is too low. Cut your expenses, if necessary. Before you had a written budget, it was hard to know where your money went each month. Now that you have a budget, it might be apparent that you are spending too much on food, or that you are spending too much on entertainment, or even that a roommate is stealing money. Do what you need to do to cut back the expenses that need cutting. Increase your income, if necessary. You might find from your budget that your expenses aren't out of line. You live in as cheap a place as possible, you eat inexpensively, you don't go out to eat, etc. In this case, the problem isn't your spending, it is your income. In order to stay out of debt, you'll need to increase your income (get a job). I know that you said that this will slow your studies, but because you are now budgeting, you have an advantage you didn't have before: you now know how short you are each month. You can take a part time job that will earn you just enough income to remain debt free while maximizing your study time. Build up a small emergency fund. Emergencies that you didn't plan for in your budget happen. To remain debt free, you should have some money set aside to cover something like this, so you don't have to borrow when it comes up. The general rule of thumb is 3 to 6 months of expenses, but as a college kid with low expenses and no family to take care of, you won't need a huge fund. $500 to $1000 extra in the bank to cover an unexpected emergency expense could be all it takes to keep you debt free.

Empirical evidence is evidence that is based on direct observation or experience. It is evidence that you can see, hear, touch, smell, or taste. For example, if you observe a tree and see that it has leaves, that is empirical evidence that the tree is a deciduous tree. Circumstantial evidence is evidence that indirectly supports a conclusion. It is evidence that suggests something is true, but does not prove it directly. For example, if you see a tree and it is autumn, that is circumstantial evidence that the tree is a deciduous tree (because deciduous trees lose their leaves in the autumn). Empirical evidence is generally considered to be better than circumstantial evidence because it is more direct and concrete. However, both types of evidence can be useful in understanding a situation or in making a case.

There are a couple of tricks you can use involving the parallax effect, measuring an object from two different locations to attempt to triangulate it's position, though that becomes less effective the further away it is. There's also a doppler effect which helps us: The further away an object is, the faster it's moving away from us. No matter which direction, that rule holds up. If that's confusing to you, try to imagine the universe as a balloon that's expanding, and we're a dot, placed on the surface of the balloon using a sharpie. Another star is another dot. As you blow more air into the balloon, everything gets further apart. But these tools eventually break down for sufficiently distant objects, and it's hard to tell the difference between a nearby red, dim star, and a far away bright bluer star. For those objects there is a miracle in Cosmology, known as the Type Ia Supernova. It's a little complicated to explain, but basically it works like this: Let's say you've got a binary star system. (There are lots of those.) And let's say one star is more massive than the other. (Lots of those, too.) Now let's say the bigger star has already burned out into a White Dwarf. There are lots of those as well. Now, if the bigger star has burned out, the smaller star probably has not. That's because the larger a star is, the * shorter * it's lifetime. The big stars burn hotter and faster. Now, you've got this binary system, where one White Dwarf circles a hydrogen-helium sister. The gravity from the White Dwarf is massive, so the orbit's likely to decay from tidal forces. Eventually the White Dwarf is going to start siphoning hydrogen off the surface of it's sister. Now, as it does, it immediately fuses that hydrogen off it's surface into more carbon & oxygen, which is what White Dwarfs are made of. And it starts getting more massive. The White Dwarf continually accretes mass until it hits a point known as * Chandrasekhar mass *, (it's very very close to, but not exactly equal to the * Chandrasekhar LIMIT *) which is the limit where electron degeneracy can no longer hold back the collapse of the star. Now here's the magical part: At that moment, an infinitesimally short time before hitting the limit, that White Dwarf star is 100% * * degenerate matter * *. That means every atom in the star is in precisely the same quantum state. Or, at least, they're all in the absolutely lowest quantum state possible for each atom. Why is this relevant? Because the moment the White Dwarf crosses the * Chandrasekhar mass *, * * every single atom in the star undergoes fusion at once! * * This is a massive, amazingly energetic explosion, that totally obliterates not only the White Dwarf, not only the sister star, but also the solar system they live in. But most importantly, because every White Dwarf that crosses that limit has exactly the same mass, * * EVERY TYPE Ia SUPERNOVA IS EXACTLY THE SAME! * * They all look alike in spectrum and magnitude, and we can calculate what they look like! So this wonderful supernova, where every single one looks exactly the same, gives us a perfect calibration tool to determine how far away they are. We look at the spectrum, realize it looks like type Ia, only redshifted by some amount, and we calculate the amount of redshift, which tells us how far away it is. We can also compare these Ia's to other stars nearby to determine what's in front of them, and what's behind.

> The local phone company offers 40mbps- just mind boggling to me that they're able to achieve that throughput on a regular telephone line. It's all about bandwidth. That is the range of frequencies you can use for communication. Higher speeds have been mostly about getting closer (and the occasional EM black magic). Early dial up systems used 3000 hz of bandwidth, which is what a long distance phone call uses. This gave a theoretical limit of 30kbps (28.8 kbps modems were typical). You couldn't go faster because the phone system only provided 3000 Hz of bandwidth, this was plenty for human voice communication. If you used frequencies lower than 400 Hz or higher than 3400 Hz the telephone system that carried dial up would just cut off the extra. Later, we got a little cleverer. You could install the dial up receiver in the exchange, before it went onto the long distance network (which has the 3000Hz limit). This allowed you to use more frequency and 56k Dial Up was born. However higher frequencies don't travel as well, so you still had an upper limit to how much bandwidth you could put through the phone line. To get closer ISPs installed cabinets closer to people's homes, this allowed them to use much more bandwidth in the existing copper cables, because the signals didn't travel as far. ADSL was born using over * 1 million Hz * of bandwidth (~25kHz-1100 kHz). The downside is that while dial up could run for a very long distance, ADSL drops off quite quickly. ADSL speeds decrease significantly after 2 km. ADSL2 + is faster, but drops off rapidly after ~1.5 km. VDSL2 + is the faster, offering up to 60mbps, but speed drops dramatically after just ~500meters.

If a player did not meet their bid, they are "set" and lose 10 points for each trick they bid. The game continues with additional rounds until one player reaches a score of at least 100 points. A bubble happens because of speculation. If people notice that the price of something has been rising consistently, they will think "hey, I can buy this now and then sell it again after the price has risen to make some money." They make the investment decision based on the assumption that the price will keep rising. Let's say the price does keep rising. More and more people will catch on that they can make some money from this investment, and will act accordingly. However, what happens with a bubble is that the price is no longer rising because the real value of the investment is increasing; instead, the price is rising because all these people keep investing in it. So, eventually whatever they're investing in becomes WAY overvalued. Once enough people start realizing that it's overvalued, there will be a rush to sell the investment (because they don't think the price will rise anymore). This starts a chain reaction of more and more selling. With all these sellers panicking and not enough buyers, the whole thing becomes unstable and collapses. Hope this is helpful!

It's calculated by adding the number of singles, two times the number of doubles, three times the number of triples, and four times the number of home runs hit by a player, and dividing that total by the number of times that player has come up to bat (also known as their at-bats). For example, let's say a player named Joe has come up to bat 100 times in a season. He has hit 20 singles, 10 doubles, 5 triples, and 2 home runs. To calculate his slugging percentage, we would do the following: Add up the total number of bases that Joe has gotten from his hits: 20 singles * 1 base + 10 doubles * 2 bases + 5 triples * 3 bases + 2 home runs * 4 bases = 80 bases, Divide the number of bases by the number of at-bats: 80 bases / 100 at-bats = 0.8 Convert the decimal to a percentage by multiplying by 100: 0.8 * 100 = 80%, So, Joe's slugging percentage for the season would be 80%. The higher the slugging percentage, the more powerful the hitter is considered to be.

I spent a few years pouring wine for a living and the quickest way I found to match wine and food is to judge the wine on two things, both of which relate to the ever elusive concept of "mouthfeel": * * * Body:* * Full or light. This basically refers to the richness and intensity of flavor. A difficult thing to describe, but you'll know it when you drink it. * * * Dry / Sweet * *: The tannins / acidity of the wine. More tannins / acidity = drier. More ripe fruit / residual sugar = sweeter. If you imagine each of these categories as an axis on a table, you get a quick and dirty way to judge wines. Just sticking with grape-types (varietals) you can shove the most common US types of wine into easy groups: * * Red * * * Light / Sweet: Pinot Noir * Light / Dry: Merlot * Full / Sweet: Zinfandel, Syrah / Shiraz * Full / Dry: Cabernet Sauvignon * * White * * * Light / Sweet: Pinot Grigio, Riesling * Light / Dry: Sauvignon Blanc * Full / Sweet: Chardonnay * Full / Dry: Chenin Blanc / Viognier (Not really a good mainstream US choice, sorry) The first thing you should know is that these groupings, like most broad descriptions of varietals, are complete and utter bullshit. The same grape can make enormously different different wines depending on where they are grown and how they are made into wine (vinified, yes it's a word). A straight syrah from Bordeaux is pretty innocuous, but a shiraz (same grape, diff name) from Australia is engineered to punch you in the face and steal your car. Similarly, most rieslings in the States tend to be on the light / sweet side, but a lot of the traditional German styles are amazingly crisp and dry. I've gone with kind of the stereotypical average styles you'll find in the US, where the whites are sweet and the reds are bold and sweet. Anyway, food. So, try judging food on the same full / light & dry / sweet criteria, then select a wine that matches it. A meal of roast grouper with a side salad? Light and dry, grab a sauvignon blanc! BBQ ribs with a side of mac & cheese? Full and sweet, grab a zinfandel or shiraz. Essentially, choose a wine that is the boozy twin of whatever you're eating. Once you've got that basic concept down, you can start learning more specifics about wine styles from various regions: their individual quirks and flavors. Then you can start making more sophisticated pairings, like knowing a full & dry wine can be great with rich and fatty foods (i.e. steak), or working out how to find something that pairs well with salty or spicy food (hint: try sparkling), or finding something that pairs with chocolate (hint: nothing, it's too sweet, pour some madeira). Of course, to really get good, you'll have to drink lots and lots and lots of wine. Try making tasting notes after your first few sips to get a feel for what works for you. Also try tasting a bunch of different types in the same sitting to compare styles. Make all your friends bring a bottle (or two) over, then start drinking and discussing. You already know what a bunch of different food tastes like, right? Now you've got to learn what a bunch different wines taste like. You. Poor. Soul. Finally, not to contradict BaconPotPie (whom I would pair with a nice Montepulciano d'Abruzzi or perhaps a Cote d'Rhone, depending on the specifics of the pot pie), but I am a European wine snob. Not only do you get to poke around with more obscure styles of wine (Basque Txakoli! Sicilian Nero d'Avola! Galician Godello! Hungarian Egri Bikaver!), but their wine labeling system actually is a lot more organized than America's. Even France, which gets needlessly complicated in the details, can give you a general expectation of what you're going to be drinking simply based on region. A Bordeaux red, to be legally called a Bordeaux, has to be made from certain grapes (mostly CabSav / Merlot with some CabFranc / Syrah / Petit Verdot) in a certain style. Same with a Rioja, Vouvray, Chianti, or Vinho Verde; you can have a certain expectation of what regional style of wine you're going to get that the American focus on varietals misses. Basically, Europeans focus on the style and ignore the grape, Americans focus on the grape and ignore the style. OK, that's my parting stereotype, commence drinking.

Hangovers have a few different causes (and we aren't exactly sure about all of them) but the number one cause of a hangover is dehydration. There are other theories as well, but those are most of the main ones. The number one cure for a hangover is hydration before-and during-alcohol intake. The fed, during these times, feels the economy is growing too quickly-possibly creating a large bubble-so they constrict the economy. Any defect in the bloodstream is called an embolism-defect meaning anything that is in the bloodstream that isn't blood. When the defect is air, it is called an air embolism. You suppose the first' question' in our chain: how does the air get there in the first place. The usual candidates are medical procedures, though major injury to a blood vessel can have the same impact. Obviously, an injection is a medical procedure. Most medical procedures with a few exceptions involve the' return' side of the vascular system, ie the veins-which is by design, and has a lot of positive side effects for an AE. The effect of an AE depends on where in the circulatory system it occurs. If, as we've indicated, the embolism occurs in a vein, it will be transmitted to the heart-specifically the right Atrium. The air will then be passed by the pumping action of the atrium into the right ventricle. This is the first place where a serious problem can occur. If the quantity of air present is enough to displace a' large volume of blood' - about 100 mL-then the ventricle may become partially or totally obstructed, which would prevent the movement of blood in the body, and lead to death. If there is * not * enough air to occlude the ventricle, the air will be pumped to the lungs where it has the potential to escape the body through the same process that all other blood gases do. If the AE begins in the arterial part of the vascular system, the problem can be much more serious as it can block the flow of blood to a major organ or system (eg, the brain or heart). The reason this can occur in the arteries but not the veins is that the arteries only' narrow' in the direction of the flow of blood, and veins only' widen.' An AE in an artery would behave exactly as any other arterial blockage, and would lead to an infarction. Now, the blood is full of dissolved gases all the time (that's its primary purpose after all) - so there is an extent to which it can handle this problem. The blood has a limited capacity to dissolve air within itself, and given time the air in blood will dissolve (assuming it does not kill the patient first). Drug design, often referred to as rational drug design or simply rational design, is the inventive process of finding new medications based on the knowledge of a biological target. The drug is most commonly an organic small molecule that activates or inhibits the function of a biomolecule such as a protein, which in turn results in a therapeutic benefit to the patient. In the most basic sense, drug design involves the design of molecules that are complementary in shape and charge to the biomolecular target with which they interact and therefore will bind to it. Drug design frequently but not necessarily relies on computer modeling techniques. This type of modeling is sometimes referred to as computer-aided drug design. Finally, drug design that relies on the knowledge of the three-dimensional structure of the biomolecular target is known as structure-based drug design. In addition to small molecules, biopharmaceuticals including peptides and especially therapeutic antibodies are an increasingly important class of drugs and computational methods for improving the affinity, selectivity, and stability of these protein-based therapeutics have also been developed. The phrase "drug design" is to some extent a misnomer. A more accurate term is ligand design (i.e., design of a molecule that will bind tightly to its target). Although design techniques for prediction of binding affinity are reasonably successful, there are many other properties, such as bioavailability, metabolic half-life, side effects, etc., that first must be optimized before a ligand can become a safe and efficacious drug. These other characteristics are often difficult to predict with rational design techniques. Nevertheless, due to high attrition rates, especially during clinical phases of drug development, more attention is being focused early in the drug design process on selecting candidate drugs whose physicochemical properties are predicted to result in fewer complications during development and hence more likely to lead to an approved, marketed drug. Furthermore, in vitro experiments complemented with computation methods are increasingly used in early drug discovery to select compounds with more favorable ADME (absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion) and toxicological profiles.

Pretty long but I think it's something a five year old could maybe understand: Light has to pass through air to get to your eyes. Air isn't very thick, so it tends to pass through it pretty easily, especially compared to stuff like glass. When air is hotter, the little things called molecules that it's made out of start moving around more and get all spread out. Because some parts of the air are hotter than others the light will pass easily through some parts of the air and will have a harder job getting through the parts with more molecules. This means the light is constantly changing speed when it's going through some hot air, and because light is a wave, when it changes speed when moving at an angle, the angle that it's moving at also changes. So when you look at some hot air you're not seeing the light from behind it in nice straight lines like you normally do, you're seeing some light from below and above it being bended and pointed in a direction that you wouldn't expect it to be. The result of this is that in very hot places like deserts the light from the sky looks like it's coming from the ground, and from a distance people would think the blue patches were water, but when they got closer it would start looking like the sand that was actually there. Because people didn't really understand why this was happening, they came up with all sorts of ideas like magic or people going crazy, but it's actually just hot air making light move in unexpected directions.

This comes up every once in a while, but there's surprisingly little understanding of it. There are a few causes of the stability we feel when riding a bicycle. 1) Gyroscopic forces. Big wheels act as a gyroscope, and if you've ever played with a child's top, you know that spinning objects tend to remain fairly stable, and resist changes to the direction they are spinning in. However, you can build a bicycle with tiny wheels, and in particular, a second set of wheels spinning backwards, cancelling out the gyroscopic effects. And that bike would be perfectly stable. 2) Trail is another factor bike designers take into account when talking about stability. Basically, trail is the measurement between the point the fork of the bike is pointing at on the ground, and the point where the tire actually touches the ground. With the tire touching the ground behind where the fork is pointing, the front wheel acts like a caster (like the wheels on the front of a shopping cart). It tends to straighten out when moving forward. However, again, this isn't the full story. You can design a bike that has little to no trail, and that bike could still be perfectly stable. 3) Steering dynamics are probably the biggest reason, as far as we can tell. All stable bikes seem to steer into a fall. That means that if you lean to one side, the bike tends to steer in that direction, effectively moving the wheels back underneath you, and countering the lean. (Really it's centrifugal acceleration pushing the center of mass outward, and the tires pushing the bottom of the bike inward. Same effect, different ways of thinking about it. It's all about the intertia of the bike, and the force on the tires.) It's not perfect, try riding with no hands, it's quite easy to get out of control if you're not careful, but as far as we can tell, this is the one crucial element for a stable bike. There were a bunch of philosophers-Descartes comes to mind, but also Spinoza and a bunch of others-who went about trying to construct a grand theory of meaning. So the existentialists, and the philosophers before them, were all about tracing meaning back to the center. They just disagreed over the center-what was it, was it God or the self? Was it something else maybe? What could we know about the source of all meaning? Then came the postmodernists. Everyone else was constructing these elaborate systems of meaning, with either God or the self at the center as the ultimate source of meaning, and all meaning could be determined in some way through a relationship with the center. The postmodernists chuckled to themselves, and then blew up the center. According to the postmodernists, those sorts of broad assertions of fact / truth are meaningless and empty-in fact, the postmodernists go one step further: they say that all those assertions of truth are * inherently unstable. * What the hell does that mean? Markets serve two functions: 1-they connect buyers and sellers so if you need / want something you can get it efficiently; and 2-they help determine prices. I assume you are just a random dude sitting in America somewhere and you have no idea what a ton of Egyptian Cotton costs or is worth. Before "markets" if I transported you to an Egyptian cotton farmer's field and told you to negotiate with him for the purchase of a ton of his cotton you would have no idea what you were doing or what to offer. Today if you find yourself in need of Egyptian cotton you can purchase it as a commodity at a price that is fair based on what everyone else in the world is paying. Nice and easy. The problem with markets however is that they often set prices that do not reflect the value of what is being sold. There are a lot of people who will disagree with this and say (foolishly) that "value is whatever someone will pay". However the phenomenon of a crash is caused by this very disconnection. Prices go up for some irrational reason and they in fact go up so high that when they come down they create an inverse irrationality that pushes them below their value. Most crashes result in over-shooting the real value and there being a rebound later. The takeaway from this is just that human beings are irrational creatures and our irrationality is reflected in market prices for goods. A crash is simply the hardest form of evidence of this irrationality. Like most cognitive defects though, most people can only see it in retrospect.

Take any number c. Now build a sequence starting with 0, c, c^2 + c, (c^2 + c)^2 + c,...with each successive term given by squaring the term before and adding c. Now, if you think a little bit about this, if you start with say, c = 2, this sequence starts to get very big very fast. But if you start with something like c = (-1/2), the sequence stays small. If the sequences continues to grow without bound, we say it diverges. If it stays small, we say it is bounded. You can also allow complex numbers as values of c (a + b i) and the definition still makes plenty of sense. Now, the mandelbrot set is simply the set of c's which produce a bounded sequence. Oftentimes the points outside are colored based on how fast their sequences diverge, but the set itself is usually colored black. This picture makes it a bit easier to see it as a graph. The x axis is the real part of the number, while the y-axis represents the complex part. As for why it has a fractal shape...I'm not sure that can be ELI5'd. One thing worth noting is that if we only allow real numbers (or just numbers with no real part), the set is just an interval. To give a slightly more complicated answer than /u / snails-exe, when the same nerve cells become stimulated over and over again they become hyperpolarized. Your nerve cells work by receiving a stimulus, which if strong enough activates channels in the cell to allow in positively charged atoms (ions). The cell is naturally negative, so the ions rush in, creating a positive charge that triggers channels further down the cell, sending a charged impulse until an action by the cell is triggered. If the cell is continually triggered, this might cause the cell to allow negatively charged ions to flow in. This makes it harder to send the positively charged impulse. It requires a greater stimulus. Therefore your brain becomes unaware of the smells because the nerve impulses from your nose to your brain are no longer being sent.

These products, which are also known as financial hedges, can be used to reduce the risk of loss in a portfolio by providing a source of compensation in the event that the value of certain stocks or other securities declines. One type of stock insurance is called a put option. A put option gives the holder the right, but not the obligation, to sell a specific stock at a predetermined price (called the strike price) on or before a certain date (called the expiration date). If the stock's market price falls below the strike price, the holder can exercise the option and sell the stock at the higher strike price, effectively insuring the value of their investment. The mathematical rule that creates the Mandelbrot set is relatively simple (at least, if you're comfortable with complex numbers from a decent algebra class). It works like this: Pick a complex number * c *. Let's say we pick c=1. Once you've picked it, start with zero and repeat the following process: square the previous number, than add * c * to it. In this case, we'd generate the sequence 0, 1 (0 ^ 2 + 1), 2 (1 ^ 2 + 1), 5 (2 ^ 2 + 1), 26 (5 ^ 2 + 1), and so on, and this sequence runs off to infinity. On the other hand, if we picked c=-1, the sequence would go 0, -1 (0 ^ 2 + -1), 0 ((-1)^2 + -1), -1, 0, -1..., and never runs off to infinity. The Mandelbrot set is the set of all numbers that do * not * run off to infinity this way.

Actually the process of German reunification while extremely costly and not without its problems did go relatively smoothly. A Korean unification by comparison would be orders of magnitude harder. It should be obvious that four guys pooling their resources to lift another guy up will have an easier time doing it than if there were just two of them trying the same thing. Another thing that gets often forgotten is that while East Germany was poor compared to West Germany, they were still one of the richest countries of communist block, having relatively high standards of living. Lifting East Germany technologically up to the level of West Germany was a monumental task, but the gap between the two countries was small compared to the gap between North and South Korea. There were plenty of people who remembered what it had been like before the division and people kept writing letters to their cousins and were even allowed to visit sometimes. It will be a lot harder to reintegrate someone from North Korea into polite society as they seem to have less of a clue about how the world actually works. All in all reuniting North and South Korea would be a far more daunting tasks than it was to reunificate Germany. Germany is one of the richest country in the world and their tasks was much easier. What you are asking about is geolocation-that is, mapping an IP address (which is a non-physical entity) to a physical location. When a service such as Amazon or Netflix wants to determine where you are located, they refer to a geolocation database-a list of IP addresses matched to real-world addresses. The most popular geolocation database that I know of is MaxMind. How does MaxMind get this information? Well, from whois lookups. Each region in the world has an IP registry-this is a body tasked with distributing blocks of IP addresses to service providers and companies. In the US, this body is called ARIN. As part of this work, ARIN operates a "whois" database (who is this IP address?). When an ISP assigns an IP address or block of IP addresses for a purpose, they are supposed to create a record at ARIN that then generates a whois record. These records can contain ownership details, addresses, telephone numbers, email addresses, routing details and more. From the addresses they can also generate a latitude and longitude, just as Google Maps can do when given an address. However, as a home user with a single IP address it is unlikely that your ISP will have gone to the effort of registering your IP address with your details. It would be a lot of time and work invested in something that would have little to no return. More than likely they simply have a pool of addresses-sometimes they will have a pool assigned to a city or suburb. If your ISP gives you a dynamic address (one that changes every time you reconnect or periodically) it is even more unlikely. Secondly, this would also mean that anyone would be able to look up your name, home address and other details simply from your IP address. Useful for legitimate companies, but it would be also be available to scammers, trolls and worse. So when a geolocation database is queried for your location, it is most likely just returning the location specified on the whois record for your IP address-which for most home users is just going to be somewhere nearby, or the ISP's local office or POP (Point of Presence-where your broadband service is connected to).

To add onto what has been said before...2 theories exist.. the Vascular Theory (Wolff's Theory) and the Central Sensitization Theory. 1) Vascular Theory (largely discredited-unfortunately since it makes more common sense) A wave of constriction of the small blood vessels of the brain occurs over a period of minutes (causing the initial "aura" and the common neurological symptoms of the migraine. This would explain why migraines can seem stroke-like with focal numbness, weakness, vertigo, visual loss, etc. Then a wave of dilation of those same vessels occurs causing the headache. Unfortunately current research has pretty much discredited it at this point. 2) Central Sensitization Theory (much more complex and less straight forward-which is a shame since its probably the correct one) A wave of electrical activity passes from the surface of the brain of the brain over a period of minutes (again causing the aura symptoms) and when it hits an area in the brainstem called the "central migraine generator(CMG)" (fancier names exist for the exact nuclei, but...unnecessary). When it activates the migraine sets in. This is why meds like triptans work best when taken early. Migraines are easier to stop before the CMG activates. When it activates a signal is sent which causes the release of inflammatory chemicals and blood vessel dilating chemicals. When the blood vessels dilate (in the setting of those inflammatory chemicals) the trigeminal nerve activates causing the perception of facial / head pain. The trigeminal nerve is the sensory nerve of the face. There's a bit about serotonin receptor deficiency as well but the whole things complicated enough already. As for botox, there's a component of tension headache in the pain from migraines as well, since migraines hurt like hell and patients are understandably tense. The theory is that you're taking the tension component out of the whole thing by giving botox. I hope that helps. Source: I'm a practicing neurologist

Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is a measure of the total value of all goods and services produced in a country in a given year. Nominal GDP measures the value of these goods and services using current prices, while real GDP measures their value using constant prices, which means that the prices of the goods and services are adjusted for inflation. Imagine that you have a basket of goods and services that you bought in two different years. The nominal GDP would measure the total cost of the basket in the current year, while the real GDP would measure the total cost of the basket in a previous year, but adjusted for inflation so that the cost is in current year dollars. Nominal GDP is useful for comparing the value of goods and services produced in different years, but it can be misleading because it doesn't account for changes in the cost of living. For example, if the prices of goods and services in a country increase from one year to the next, the nominal GDP will also increase, even if the actual quantity of goods and services produced has not changed. Real GDP, on the other hand, is useful for comparing the quantity of goods and services produced in different years, because it adjusts for changes in prices. This makes it a better measure of the overall standard of living in a country. So, in short, you would use nominal GDP when you want to compare the value of goods and services produced in different years, and you would use real GDP when you want to compare the quantity of goods and services produced in different years, adjusted for changes in prices.

There are a lot of ways to do AI for games depending on what kind of game it is and what the rules are but here's a really simple example. In tic-tac-toe there is a board with nine squares and players take turns filling squares with a nought or a cross. The game ends when one player has three symbols in a row or the board is full. In the first scenario, that player wins and the second is a draw. Since tic-tac-toe is a relatively simple game, we can come up with some really good [strategies] (#Strategy) and even make a diagram for how to win. In this kind of situation, all you need to do is put the winning moves into the computer and let it follow instructions. But how does this work? Well, for tic-tac-toe we might use a tree. Trees are easy to make in today's object-oriented languages like C #and Java. Here, the top of the tree represents the start of the game and you follow branches downwards from state to state as the game goes on. In the picture, the board starts empty and let's say the player places an X. The computer follows the branch to the appropriate state and from there it can look down subsequent branches to see what states can possibly come next. At the bottom of the tree will be all the possible end states for the game. Some of them will be kind of high up, where someone gets three in a row and some of them will be nine layers down where the board is full and it's a draw. So how do we use the tree to figure out winning moves? There are, again a few ways you could do it but let's stick with the easiest example. Let's take a look at every possible' end state' in the tree and give it a value depending on whether or not it's a good outcome for us. We could put a' 1' on every end state where we win, a' -1' on every end state where we lose and a' 0' on every end state where it's a draw. Then all we need to do is say "the value of any particular state is determined by summing the value of all the states that could come next". Let's imagine we're looking at a state where there are two possible next moves, one where we win and one where it's a draw. The win is worth 1 point and the draw is worth zero so the total value of the current state is 1. We can do this all the way back up the tree until every state of the game has an appropriate point value. Then, when we want to choose our next move, all we have to do is pick the one that has the most points because that's the one which has the most chance of ending in a win for us! Of course, this strategy doesn't work so well for complex games like chess because there is such a wide variety of moves that the tree gets really big, really quickly-too big for current computers to handle. In that kind of situation we might combine a few different AI strategies and hope for the best. For instance, we could program the computer with some preset opening gambits, some preset endgame strategies and use our tree idea to simulate the mid-game as well as possible, filling in the blanks with our best guess at how much a branch is worth. We can cover the start and end pretty thoroughly because we have more solid facts about them; at the start everyone has most of their pieces and there are only a few places they can be while at the end people might only have a few pieces to worry about and that simplifies things a lot. The middle is tricky because we can't really get a good idea of how to weigh short term gains against long term gains because we can't model every possibility but we might be able to make some educated guesses by estimating the value of the pieces in play and the value of their positions on the board. Of course, this sort of thing isn't going to make much sense for bots in an FPS but that's a whole' nother kettle of fish.

Short selling is the practice of selling securities that the seller does not own, with the expectation that the price of the securities will decline. In order to sell securities that the seller does not own, the seller must borrow the securities from someone else. The seller then sells the borrowed securities on the market and hopes to buy them back at a lower price in the future. If the price of the securities does indeed decline, the seller can buy them back at the lower price and return them to the lender, pocketing the difference as profit. If the price of the securities increases instead, the seller will have to buy them back at a higher price and will incur a loss. Borrowing the securities is typically done through a broker, who will arrange for the securities to be borrowed from another investor or institution that owns them. The broker may charge a fee for this service. In order to borrow the securities, the short seller must also provide collateral to the lender, usually in the form of cash or other securities. This is to ensure that the lender will be able to recover the value of the borrowed securities if the price goes up instead of down, and the short seller is unable to buy them back at a profit.

Ex post facto laws are laws that retroactively change the legal consequences of actions that were taken before the law was passed. These types of laws are often used to criminalize actions that were not illegal at the time they were committed, or to increase the punishment for actions that were already illegal. For example, imagine that you live in a country where it is not illegal to steal a small amount of money from someone. If you stole a small amount of money before the new law was passed, and you are caught after the law is passed, you could be punished even though you didn't know that what you were doing was illegal at the time. This would be an example of an ex post facto law. Ex post facto laws are generally considered to be unfair because they can punish people for actions that they thought were legal at the time, and because they can increase the punishment for actions that have already been committed. In many countries, including the United States, ex post facto laws are specifically prohibited by the constitution.

Maria, there are a few questions I think you must consider when considering this problem. Do fundamental or technical strategies provide meaningful information? Are the signals they produce actionable? In my experience, and many quantitative traders will probably say similar things, technical analysis is unlikely to provide anything meaningful. Of course you may find phenomena when looking back on data and a particular indicator, but this is often after the fact. One cannot action-ably trade these observations. On the other hand, it does seem that fundamentals can play a crucial role in the overall (typically long run) dynamics of stock movement. Here are two examples, Technical: suppose we follow stock X and buy every time the price crosses above the 30 day moving average. There is one obvious issue with this strategy - why does this signal have significance? If the method is designed arbitrarily then the answer is that it does not have significance. Moreover, much of the research supports that stocks move close to a geometric brownian motion with jumps. This supports the implication that the system is meaningless - if the probability of up or down is always close to 50/50 then why would an average based on the price be predictive? Fundamental: Suppose we buy stocks with the best P/E ratios (defined by some cutoff). This makes sense from a logical perspective and may have some long run merit. However, there is always a chance that an internal blowup or some macro event creates a large loss. A blended approach: for sake of balance perhaps we consider fundamentals as a good long-term indication of growth (what quants might call drift). We then restrict ourselves to equities in a particular index - say the S&P500. We compare the growth of these stocks vs. their P/E ratios and possibly do some regression. A natural strategy would be to sell those which have exceeded the expected return given the P/E ratio and buy those which have underperformed. Since all equities we are considering are in the same index, they are most likely somewhat correlated (especially when traded in baskets). If we sell 10 equities that are deemed "too high" and buy 10 which are "too low" we will be taking a neutral position and betting on convergence of the spread to the market average growth. We have this constructed a hedged position using a fundamental metric (and some helpful statistics). This method can be categorized as a type of index arbitrage and is done (roughly) in a similar fashion. If you dig through some data (yahoo finance is great) over the past 5 years on just the S&P500 I'm sure you'll find plenty of signals (and perhaps profitable if you calibrate with specific numbers). Sorry for the long and rambling style but I wanted to hit a few key points and show a clever methods of using fundamentals.

When you are driving by a siren, the pitch of the sound seems to change because of something called the Doppler effect. The Doppler effect is a change in the frequency or pitch of a sound wave that occurs when the source of the sound and the listener are moving relative to each other. For example, when a siren on an ambulance is approaching you, the sound waves it is emitting are compressed, or squeezed together. This makes the pitch of the siren sound higher. As the ambulance passes by you and moves away, the sound waves it is emitting are stretched out, which makes the pitch of the siren sound lower. This is similar to what happens when a car with a loud horn drives by you. The pitch of the horn seems to change as the car approaches and then moves away from you. So, when you are driving by a siren, the pitch of the sound seems to change because the source of the sound (the ambulance or fire truck) is moving relative to you, and the Doppler effect causes the pitch of the sound to change.

Principal component analysis (PCA) is a statistical technique that is used to reduce the dimensionality of a data set. It does this by identifying the directions in which the data varies the most, and then projecting the data onto a new set of axes that are orthogonal (perpendicular) to each other. These new axes are called "principal components", and they are ranked in order of importance, with the first principal component having the highest importance and the last principal component having the lowest importance. The purpose of PCA is to find a low-dimensional representation of the data that captures as much of the variance in the data as possible. This can be useful for visualizing the data, or for finding patterns in the data that might not be apparent in the original high-dimensional space. To perform PCA, you first need to standardize the data by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation. Then, you compute the covariance matrix of the data, and use singular value decomposition (SVD) to decompose the covariance matrix into its principal components. Finally, you can select the number of principal components to keep, and project the data onto the resulting low-dimensional space.PCA is a widely used technique in data analysis and machine learning, and it has many applications, including feature selection, dimensionality reduction, and data visualization.

Exchange-traded funds (ETFs) are investment vehicles that allow you to buy or sell shares in a basket of securities. ETFs are similar to mutual funds in that they both offer investors exposure to a diverse range of assets, but they trade on stock exchanges and can be bought and sold throughout the day like individual stocks. One of the key features of ETFs is that they typically have low fees compared to other types of investment vehicles. These fees are often referred to as the "expense ratio," which is the annual fee that the ETF charges its shareholders for its management and other expenses. The expense ratio is expressed as a percentage of the value of the assets in the ETF and is deducted from the returns earned by the ETF.For example, if an ETF has an expense ratio of 0.5% and you have invested $10,000 in the ETF, the annual fee that you would pay would be $50 ($10,000 x 0.5%). This fee would be deducted from the returns earned by the ETF, so the actual return that you receive would be lower than the return earned by the ETF before the fees were applied. In addition to the expense ratio, ETFs may also charge other fees, such as trading fees when you buy or sell shares in the ETF. These fees are generally much smaller than the expense ratio and may be waived by some brokers. It's important to carefully consider the fees that an ETF charges before you invest in it, as they can have a significant impact on your returns over the long term. You can typically find information about the fees that an ETF charges in its prospectus or on the website of the company that manages the ETF.

ADEM (acute disseminated encephalomyelitis) is a rare, autoimmune disorder that affects the brain and spinal cord. It is characterized by the sudden onset of symptoms such as fever, fatigue, and neurological problems, including difficulty with movement, balance, and coordination. ADEM is thought to be triggered by a viral or bacterial infection, or sometimes by a vaccination, and it is characterized by inflammation and damage to the myelin sheath, the protective covering that surrounds nerve fibers in the brain and spinal cord. The severity of ADEM can range from mild to severe, and it can lead to long-term neurological problems or even death in some cases. Treatment for ADEM typically involves the use of corticosteroids or other immunosuppressive medications to reduce inflammation and prevent further damage to the brain and spinal cord.

When two gas stations are located across the street from each other, they are in what is called "direct competition" with each other. This means that they are both selling the same product (gasoline) to the same group of customers (people who live or work in the area). In order to attract customers, one gas station might try to lower its prices below those of the other gas station. This is called "undercutting." However, if one gas station were to constantly lower its prices, it might not make enough money to stay in business. Additionally, if one gas station were to lower its prices significantly, the other gas station might feel pressure to lower its prices as well. This could lead to a "price war," where both gas stations are constantly trying to outdo each other by lowering their prices. In the end, both gas stations could end up making less money. To avoid this situation, it is often more profitable for gas stations to "match" the prices of their direct competitors, rather than constantly trying to undercut each other. ----- ###Introduction. ----- In Formal Logic, we have * variables * and * connectives *. * Variables * act in logic similar to how they act in algebra; they can either be True (* * T * *) or False (* * F * *). * Connectives * in logic take those variables, and depending on the variables' truth values, they output another truth value. ----- ###Basic connectives. ----- The three basic connectives are * * OR * *, * * AND * *, and * * NOT * *. Let's start with * * OR * *. We have the statement x * * OR * * y, where x and y are the variables. x * * OR * * y is T when either * x * or * y * is T; otherwise, it's false. |**x**|**y**|**x OR y**| |:------------:|:------------:|:------------:| |T|T|T| |T|F|T| |F|T|T| |F|F|F| (The above is a truth table; you'll see these a lot in Formal Logic. They're basically all the possible combinations of truth values of the variables, and the outputs in each case.) x * * AND * * y is T if both * x * and * y * are T, and F otherwise. |**x**|**y**|**x AND y**| |:------------:|:------------:|:------------:| |T|T|T| |T|F|F| |F|T|F| |F|F|F| * * NOT * * is different. * * AND * * and * * OR * * operate on two variables; * * NOT * * operates on one. It switches the truth value of the variable it's working on. For example, if * x * is T, * * * NOT * * x * is F. |**x**|**NOT x**| |:------------:|:------------:| |T|F| |F|T| ----- ###Advanced connectives. ----- There are other connectives, such as * * XOR * *, * * XNOR * *, and * * NAND * *. The * * OR * * operator uses the * inclusive * definition of "or," meaning that it's not an either-or case. If you're asked if you want sprinkles or cherry cream on your icecream, it's inclusive, which means that you can have both. But in * * XOR * * the * exclusive * definition of "or" applies; you can only have one. Here is its truth table: |**x**|**y**|**x XOR y**| |:------------:|:------------:|:------------:| |T|T|F| |T|F|T| |F|T|T| |F|F|F| * * XNOR * * is the opposite of * * XOR * *: It outputs T if both inputs have the same truth value, and F otherwise. |**x**|**y**|**x XNOR y**| |:------------:|:------------:|:------------:| |T|T|T| |T|F|F| |F|T|F| |F|F|T| * * NAND * * outputs F if both its inputs are T, and T otherwise. |**x**|**y**|**x NAND y**| |:------------:|:------------:|:------------:| |T|T|F| |T|F|T| |F|T|T| |F|F|T| ----- ###Equivalence and adequacy. ----- You can see why we need the basic connectives for basic things. But why do we need * * NAND * *? There's something called * equivalence *: If two statements have the same truth table, they're * equivalent *, which means that they're the same. For example, x * * XNOR * * y is equivalent to * * NOT * * (x * * XOR * * y) because their truth tables are opposite, and to equate one to the other you put * * NOT * * to flip the truth value of one of them. Another concept in logic is * adequacy *. There are an infinite amount of truth tables from different combinations of variables and truth tables; but we can construct any truth table we want with statements and a * finite * number of logical connectives. The basic operators (* * NOT * *, * * OR * *, and * * AND * *) are sufficient to make a statement for every truth table in existence. So are * * NOT * * and either * * OR * * or * * AND * *. * x * * AND * * y * is the same as * * NOT * * ((* * NOT**x) * * OR * * (* * NOT**y)) - see it by constructing the truth tables of both statements and comparing them. Then, to prove that a set of logical connectives is adequate, we should prove that the truth tables generated * just * by those connectives are equivalent to * * NOT * * x * and x * * AND * * y. * * NAND * * and * * XOR * * have a special property of being adequate alone. Let's take * * NAND * * as an example. |**x**|**x NAND x**| |:------------:|:------------:| |T|F| |F|T| Isn't this the same truth table as * * NOT * *? And if you notice, if you add a * * NOT * * to the final statement in * * NAND * *'s truth table, it flips the signs, and lo! It's the same as that of * * AND * *. So * * NOT * * (x * * NAND * * y) is equivalent to x * * AND * * x.

Fractional reserve banking and Ponzi schemes are two different financial systems or practices that have some similarities, but are also quite different in important ways. Fractional reserve banking is a system that banks use to manage deposits and loans. Under this system, banks are required to keep a certain percentage of their deposits on hand as reserves, while they can lend out the rest of the money to borrowers. For example, if a bank has $100 in deposits and is required to keep 10% as reserves, it can lend out $90 to borrowers. The idea behind fractional reserve banking is to allow banks to make more loans and earn more money from interest, while still being able to meet the demands of depositors who might want to withdraw their money at any time.A Ponzi scheme, on the other hand, is a fraudulent investment scheme in which earlier investors are paid with the investments of more recent investors, rather than with actual profits earned. In a Ponzi scheme, the person running the scheme (the "operator") promises high returns to investors, but instead of using the investment money to generate profits, the operator simply takes the money and uses it to pay earlier investors. This creates the illusion of a profitable investment, and can continue for a while as long as more and more people are willing to invest. However, eventually the scheme collapses because there is not enough money to pay all the investors, and the operator usually ends up disappearing with the remaining funds. So, while both fractional reserve banking and Ponzi schemes involve the use of other people's money to generate profits, fractional reserve banking is a legitimate and regulated financial system that is intended to be transparent and fair, while Ponzi schemes are fraudulent and deceitful, and are designed to take advantage of people's trust and greed.

There's no one best answer to this-every operating system does it a little differently. You can read about the algorithm used in the Linux kernel by searching for Linux "Completely Fair Scheduler" (that's the name of the algorithm, since 2010 or so). The theory behind this algorithm is that you have two basic types of processes: interactive and non-interactive. Interactive processes are programs you're using, like your web browser, word processor, etc. - they normally sit there doing nothing, until you press a key or click with the mouse, then they're really busy. In contrast, other programs might be busy in the background, doing things like encoding a DVD, backing up your hard disk, and downloading a torrent. These processes are non-interactive, their goal is to get a lot of work done, not to be responsive. The "Completely Fair Scheduler" works by giving higher priority to tasks that haven't used a lot of cpu time recently. So this automatically makes interactive processes more responsive-when a program sits around doing nothing while it waits for you to press a key, then when you do press a key it becomes the highest priority process until it's done processing the key. In contrast, a DVD encoding process steals all available idle cpu time, so when you press a key in your mail reader, the DVD encoding process temporarily becomes much lower priority until your mail reader is done.

If you can measure the coordinates (longitude and latitude) of points on Earth, you can plot an accurate map by following the shore, taking measurements at various points, putting them on a map and connecting the points. The way I see it, the challenges to ancient map makers would have fallen under two categories. First: did they understand the shape of the Earth accurately? You need to understand that the Earth is a sphere (more or less) to make accurate large-scale maps that fit a whole continent. For example, somebody who believes that the the Earth is flat is going to run into the problem that north-south lines aren't parallel-they meet at the poles. The ancient Greeks figured out that the Earth is (roughly) spherical; Erathostenes and Hipparchus had an understanding of longitude and latitude as well, a couple of centuries BC. Admiral Zheng He was a Muslim, and Islamic scholars had translated and taught ancient Greek knowledge for centuries, so you can bet he knew this stuff. Second challenge: did the ancients have a good way to measure the coordinates of a spot on Earth? Latitude is relatively easy, because you can figure it out from the sun or the stars. For example, you can use the angle between the horizon and the north star. But there was no accurate and reliable method of measuring longitude on land until the late 1600s, and longitude at sea didn't get solved until the late 1700s. Before this, what people did was to guess the longitude using (a) distance from a known point, (b) latitude and (c) an estimate of the size of the Earth. These estimates, however, were wrong all the time. So when you look at any large-scale map made before 1650 or so, you can be pretty sure that the latitudes are right but the longitudes are wrong. If you're curious or adventurous, you see this easily by comparing old maps to modern ones; for example, in this /r / MapPorn comment I compare a 1635 map of Africa to modern maps, and the longitudes are wrong:> The longitudes, as is to be expected, are way off. This concept is well explored in a book (and I believe TV series now too) called Guns, Germs, and Steel. I would urge you to read / watch it if you ever find time. It should be taken with a grain of salt, but it does posit a number of very good theories. Essentially what it boils down to (at least in that particular author's opinion), is food supply. The agricultural revolution in Europe led to more efficient farming methods that required less work for more food. Less work equals more time, more time leads to boredom, boredom leads to curiosity, et cetera. Only very recently (as far as human history is concerned) has Europe held such dominance in technology. It should also be noted that Europe rose to power in the form of Rome and Macedonia, but also collapsed into the Dark Ages before re-rising to power in the modern context. A great deal of Europe's post-Dark Ages society is based on science and math kept alive by the Arabs (algebra and trigonometry, among others), and wouldn't have been possible without the Crusades bringing a lot of that information back. So I guess the simplest explanation is probably pure luck. Of all the incredibly powerful civilizations that rose up and fell throughout history, Europe managed to do so right on the cusp of the Industrial Revolution and rise of globalization, ensuring their global dominance in the modern age. Your blood type is based on what proteins are present on the surface of your red blood cells. There are three types of proteins we're interested in. We will call these proteins A, B and Rh. You can have all of these proteins, none of them, or any combination. The letter part of your blood type is determined by the A and B proteins. If you have both types, you are AB. If you only have A, you are A, only B is B. If you have neither A nor B, you are type O. O means "lacks both A and B." The + or-on your blood type is based on the Rh protein. If you have the Rh protein, you are Rh positive, which gives you a + on your blood type. If you do not have the Rh protein, you are Rh negative, and get a-on your blood type. A-is similar to type O. It just means your blood does not contain this protein. Your immune system will attack anything it doesn't recognize. That includes blood cells. As long as the blood cells in a transfusion do not have anything your body does not recognize, your body will accept it. If your body sees a protein it does not recognize, it will attack the new blood cells. For example, if you are B+ and you get any type of blood with the A protein in it, your body will attack the new blood. As long as the new blood does not contain A, it will work just fine. This means a B+ can accept B-, O+, etc., but not A-, AB+, etc. This is why O- is called a "universal donor". O- blood can be given to anybody. The immune system of a B+ person will look at the O- blood and say, "I don't see anything here I don't recognize" and leave it alone. This makes O- blood more in demand, because if someone in an emergency room needs a blood transfusion, and there's no chance to find out the blood type, they have to use O- to be safe. This also makes it sort of nice to be AB+, because an AB+ can receive blood from any donor.

I'm not sure there's a good reason to do a "closing the books" ceremony for personal finance accounting. (And you're not only wanting to do that, but have a fiscal year that's different from the calendar year? Yikes!) My understanding is that usually this process is done for businesses to be able to account for what their "Retained Earnings" and such are for investors and tax purposes; generally individuals wouldn't think of their finances in those terms. It's certainly not impossible, though. Gnucash, for example, implements a "Closing Books" feature, which is designed to create transactions for each Income and Expenses account into an end-of-year Equity Retained Earnings account. It doesn't do any sort of closing out of Assets or Liabilities, however. (And I'm not sure how that would make any sense, as you'd transfer it from your Asset to the End-of-year closing account, and then transfer it back as an Opening Balance for the next year?) If you want to keep each year completely separate, the page about Closing Books in the Gnucash Wiki mentions that one can create a separate Gnucash file per year by exporting the account tree from your existing file, then importing that tree and the balances into a new file. I expect that it makes it much more challenging to run reports across multiple years of data, though. While your question doesn't seem to be specific to Gnucash (I just mention it because it's the accounting tool I'm most familiar with), I'd expect that any accounting program would have similar functionality. I would, however, like to point out this section from the Gnucash manual: Note that closing the books in GnuCash is unnecessary. You do not need to zero out your income and expense accounts at the end of each financial period. GnuCash's built-in reports automatically handle concepts like retained earnings between two different financial periods. In fact, closing the books reduces the usefulness of the standard reports because the reports don't currently understand closing transactions. So from their point of view it simply looks like the net income or expense in each account for a given period was simply zero. And that's largely why I'm just not sure what your goals are. If you want to look at your transactions for a certain time, to "just focus on the range of years I'm interested in for any given purpose" as you say, then just go ahead and run the report you care about with those years as the dates. The idea of "closing books" comes from a time when you'd want to take your pile of paper ledgers and go put them in storage once you didn't need to refer to them regularly. Computers now have no challenges storing "every account from the beginning of time" at all, and you can filter out that data to focus on whatever you're looking for easily. If you don't want to look at the old data, just don't include them in your reports. I'm pretty sure that's the "better way to keep the books manageable".

Latino = Shorthand for "latinoamericano", in other words Latin-American. It is the term used for the people in the New World descending culturally, linguistically, or ethnically from the Old World explorers of Romance language countries (Spain, Portugal, Italy, France, Romania, Andorra, Monaco, I may be forgetting a couple.) Since out of those countries it was only really Spain, Portugal, and France which held colonies in the New World, those are the ones that matter in this case. So a "Latino" is, generally speaking, anyone from any of those former colonies. Technically, Brazil (Portuguese colony), Haiti (French colony), and Quebec (French colony) fall into this category, however you won't really hear people from those places call themselves Latino / Latin-American (toss-up for Brazil, I've heard Brazilians on numerous occasions refer to themselves as Latino). It has become a term which in practice means those from former Spanish colonies in the Americas. Even then, not all of them refer to themselves as Latino and opt for the term Hispanic. Hispanic = Culturally, linguistically, or ethnically originating from Spain. In this sense, all Hispanic countries with the exception of Spain (and potentially the Philippines, though I honestly don't know how they classify themselves) are Latin-American. At the same time, some people prefer the term Hispanic over Latino whereas others prefer the inverse. For example, an Argentinean would generally prefer being called Hispanic to Latino, and a Mexican would prefer Latino to Hispanic. A lot of the time it comes down to "how Spanish" they feel they are. The typical Argentinean is "more Spanish" (by blood at least) than the typical Mexican who is usually of mixed ancestry (Spanish and indigenous.) Overall, it's probably a safer bet to go with Latino (better yet, Latin-American) over Hispanic, but keep in mind many prefer the other term.

Medical diagnosis (abbreviated Dx, Dx, or Ds) is the process of determining which disease or condition explains a person's symptoms and signs. It is most often referred to as diagnosis with the medical context being implicit. The information required for diagnosis is typically collected from a history and physical examination of the person seeking medical care. Often, one or more diagnostic procedures, such as medical tests, are also done during the process. Sometimes posthumous diagnosis is considered a kind of medical diagnosis. Diagnosis is often challenging because many signs and symptoms are nonspecific. For example, redness of the skin (erythema), by itself, is a sign of many disorders and thus does not tell the healthcare professional what is wrong. Thus differential diagnosis, in which several possible explanations are compared and contrasted, must be performed. This involves the correlation of various pieces of information followed by the recognition and differentiation of patterns. Occasionally the process is made easy by a sign or symptom (or a group of several) that is pathognomonic. Diagnosis is a major component of the procedure of a doctor's visit. To add to @keshlam's answer slightly a stock's price is made up of several components: the only one of these that is known even remotely accurately at any time is the book value on the day that the accounts are prepared. Even completed cashflows after the books have been prepared contain some slight unknowns as they may be reversed if stock is returned, for example, or reduced by unforeseen costs. Future cashflows are based on (amongst other things) how many sales you expect to make in the future for all time. Exercise for the reader: how many iPhone 22s will apple sell in 2029? Even known future cashflows have some risk attached to them; customers may not pay for goods, a supplier may go into liquidation and so need to change its invoicing strategy etc.. Estimating the risk on future cashflows is highly subjective and depends greatly on what the analyst expects the exact economic state of the world will be in the future. Investors have the choice of investing in a risk free instrument (this is usually taken as being modelled by the 10 year US treasury bond) that is guaranteed to give them a return. To invest in anything riskier than the risk free instrument they must be paid a premium over the risk free return that they would get from that. The risk premium is related to how likely they think it is that they will not receive a return higher than that rate. Calculation of that premium is highly subjective; if I know the management of the company well I will be inclined to think that the investment is far less risky (or perhaps riskier...) than someone who does not, for example. Since none of the factors that go into a share price are accurately measurable and many are subjective there is no "right" share price at any time, let alone at time of IPO. Each investor will estimate these values differently and so value the shares differently and their trading, based on their ever changing estimates, will move the share price to an indeterminable level. In comments to @keshlam's answer you ask if there is enough information to work out the share price if a company buys out the company before IPO. Dividing the price that this other company paid by the relative ownership structure of the firm would give you an idea of what that company thought that the company was worth at that moment in time and can be used as a surrogate for market price but it will not and cannot accurately represent the market price as other investors will value the firm differently by estimating the criteria above differently and so will move the share price based on their valuation.

In general economic theory, there are always two markets created based on a need for a good; a spot market (where people who need something now can go outbid other people who need the same thing), and a futures market (where people who know they will need something later can agree to buy it for a pre-approved price, even if the good in question doesn't exist yet, like a grain crop). Options exist as a natural extension of the futures market. In a traditional future, you're obligated, by buying the contract, to execute it, for good or ill. If it turns out that you could have gotten a lower price when buying, or a higher price when selling, that's tough; you gave up the ability to say no in return for knowing, a month or three months or even a year in advance, the price you'll get to buy or sell this good that you know you need. Futures thus give both sides the ability to plan based on a known price, but that's their only risk-reduction mechanism. Enter the option. You're the Coors Brewing Company, and you want to buy 50 tons of barley grain for delivery in December in order to brew up for the Super Bowl and other assorted sports parties. A co-op bellies up to close the deal. But, since you're Coors, you compete on price with Budweiser and Miller, and if you end up paying more than the grain's really worth, perhaps because of a mild wet fall and a bumper crop that the almanac predicts, then you're going to have a real bad time of it in January. You ask for the right to say "no" when the contract falls due, if the price you negotiate now is too high based on the spot price. The co-op now has a choice; for such a large shipment, if Coors decided to leave them holding the bag on the contract and instead bought it from them anyway on a depressed spot market, they could lose big if they were counting on getting the contract price and bought equipment or facilities on credit against it. To mitigate those losses, the co-op asks for an option price; basically, this is "insurance" on the contract, and the co-op will, in return for this fee (exactly how and when it's paid is also negotiable), agree to eat any future realized losses if Coors were to back out of the contract. Like any insurance premium, the option price is nominally based on an outwardly simple formula: the probability of Coors "exercising" their option, times the losses the co-op would incur if that happened. Long-term, if these two figures are accurate, the co-op will break even by offering this price and Coors either taking the contract or exercising the option. However, coming up with accurate predictions of these two figures, such that the co-op (or anyone offering such a position) would indeed break even at least, is the stuff that keeps actuaries in business (and awake at night).

Carbon monoxide is dangerous because it can replace the oxygen in your blood, leading to a condition called carbon monoxide poisoning. When you inhale carbon monoxide, it binds to the red blood cells in your body, replacing the oxygen that would normally be carried by these cells. As a result, your body doesn't get enough oxygen, and your cells and tissues can't function properly. This can cause symptoms such as headache, dizziness, weakness, nausea, and eventually unconsciousness and death. Carbon monoxide poisoning can be especially dangerous because it is often hard to detect. Carbon monoxide is a colorless, tasteless, and odorless gas, so you might not realize you're breathing it in until it's too late. That's why it's important to be aware of the sources of carbon monoxide and to take precautions to protect yourself from it, such as using carbon monoxide detectors in your home and never using gas appliances or vehicles in poorly ventilated areas.

When you stand up quickly after sitting or laying down for an extended period of time, you may experience a temporary "blindness" or loss of vision for a few seconds. This is a common phenomenon known as "postural hypotension" or "orthostatic hypotension." It occurs when there is a sudden drop in blood pressure when you stand up, which can cause a temporary decrease in blood flow to the brain and result in dizziness or temporary loss of vision. Postural hypotension is generally not a serious condition and usually goes away on its own within a few seconds. However, it can be caused by certain medical conditions or medications, so it's always a good idea to speak with a healthcare provider if you experience this symptom frequently or if it is accompanied by other symptoms such as fainting or chest pain. To prevent postural hypotension, you can try the following tips: Stand up slowly: Avoid standing up too quickly, especially after sitting or lying down for an extended period of time. Wear compression stockings: These can help improve circulation and reduce the risk of postural hypotension. Stay hydrated: Drinking plenty of fluids can help maintain proper blood pressure. Eat a healthy diet: A diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains can help maintain healthy blood pressure. Exercise regularly: Regular exercise can help improve circulation and reduce the risk of postural hypotension. Avoid alcohol and caffeine: These can both interfere with blood pressure regulation and increase the risk of postural hypotension.

It's important to note that mortgage payments typically include both principal and interest. In double-entry accounting, the interest portion of the mortgage payment is recorded as an expense in the period in which it is paid, while the principal is recorded as a reduction in the mortgage liability. For example, let's say that your mortgage payment of $1,000 includes $800 of principal and $200 of interest. Electromagnetic waves are a type of energy that travels through the air and carries information. There are different ways to use electromagnetic waves to transmit information, such as AM (amplitude modulation) and FM (frequency modulation). In AM radio, the information is carried by changing the strength, or amplitude, of the electromagnetic wave. For example, a radio station might use a stronger wave to represent a "1" and a weaker wave to represent a "0". By sending a series of these strong and weak waves, the radio station can transmit information, such as music or a voice. In FM radio, the information is carried by changing the frequency, or pitch, of the electromagnetic wave. For example, a radio station might use a high frequency wave to represent a "1" and a low frequency wave to represent a "0". By sending a series of these high and low frequency waves, the radio station can transmit information, such as music or a voice. Both AM and FM radio use electromagnetic waves to transmit information, but they do it in different ways.

The homeowner doesn't have to make any payments on the loan as long as they continue to live in the home. When the homeowner dies, sells the home, or moves out, they or their heirs must pay back the loan, plus interest and fees. Reverse mortgages can be a helpful financial tool for certain seniors who need additional income, but they also come with risks. For example, if the homeowner doesn't make payments on their property taxes or insurance, the lender can foreclose on the home. It's important to carefully consider all of the options and fully understand the terms of a reverse mortgage before deciding to take one out.
